notes.h: Capturing light: pigments and the reaction centre (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The light-dependent reactions start when light hits a leaf. Before any chemistry can happen, the plant has to catch that light energy and channel it to one special chlorophyll molecule, which uses it to fire off an electron.
points: Light travels as tiny packets of energy called photons. A pigment is a molecule that absorbs light of particular colours (wavelengths).

The thylakoid membranes hold several pigments: chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, and yellow and orange pigments called carotenoids. Each absorbs slightly different colours, so having several widens the range of light the plant can use.

The pigment molecules sit in clusters of hundreds, called light-harvesting or antenna complexes, around a reaction centre. The cluster works like a satellite dish, collecting light over a wide area and focusing it on one point.
When any pigment in the cluster absorbs a photon, the energy is passed from one pigment molecule to the next until it reaches the reaction centre, a special chlorophyll a molecule.

At the reaction centre, the energy raises (excites) one of the chlorophyll's electrons to a high energy level. This energised electron leaves the chlorophyll and is taken up by an electron acceptor, the first carrier of an electron transport chain.
Because an electron carries a negative charge, losing one leaves the reaction-centre chlorophyll positively charged. It must get an electron back before it can fire off another one.
notes.tip: If asked what chlorophyll releases when it absorbs light, the answer is energised (high-energy) electrons. Don't say that light hits water and splits it: the light is absorbed by the pigments.

notes.b: The energised electron now has to go somewhere useful. In the non-cyclic pathway, it travels one way, from water to NADP⁺, and along the way its energy is used to make the two things the second stage of photosynthesis needs: ATP and NADPH.
points: 1. Light energy reaches the reaction centre, and energised electrons leave the chlorophyll.

2. The electrons are passed along an electron transport chain, a series of electron carriers in the thylakoid membrane. At each hand-over they lose a little energy, like a ball bouncing down a staircase, and this released energy is used to make ATP from ADP and phosphate (Pi).
3. At the end of the chain, the electrons, now at lower energy, are passed to NADP⁺, a hydrogen carrier. Each NADP⁺ takes two electrons and one proton (H⁺) to form NADPH: NADP⁺ + 2e⁻ + H⁺ → NADPH.

4. The chlorophyll is still positively charged, so it strongly attracts electrons and pulls them from water molecules. This splits the water, a step called photolysis (splitting by light, because the energy for it ultimately came from light): 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂.
5. The electrons from water replace the ones the chlorophyll lost, so it is neutral again and ready to absorb more energy.
The protons (H⁺) from photolysis are used to form NADPH, and they also help build up the proton store that drives ATP-making in the thylakoid.
The oxygen from photolysis is a by-product. It is used in the cell's respiration or released through the stomata.

It is called non-cyclic because the electrons go one way only, from water through the chlorophyll and the chain to NADP⁺, and never return to where they started. The electrons aren't used up; they end up on NADPH.
Products of the non-cyclic pathway: ATP, NADPH and oxygen.
notes.tip: A full description goes in order: light passed to the reaction centre, electrons energised and passed along the chain (ATP made), electrons and a proton taken up by NADP⁺ (NADPH made), and water split to replace the electrons (oxygen released). Write NADPH, not NADPH₂ or NADH.

notes.b: Sometimes the energised electrons take a shortcut. In the cyclic pathway they loop back to the chlorophyll they came from, making ATP on the way but nothing else.
points: In the cyclic pathway, some energised electrons leaving the reaction-centre chlorophyll pass along carriers of the electron transport chain and then return to the same chlorophyll molecule, instead of going on to NADP⁺.
As they pass along the carriers, they give up their extra energy, which is used to make ATP from ADP and Pi.
Because the electrons come back, the chlorophyll is neutral again without needing electrons from water. So water is not split, no oxygen is released and no NADPH is made.
Products of the cyclic pathway: ATP only.
Why the plant needs it: the light-independent reactions use more ATP than NADPH, 3 ATP for every 2 NADPH for each CO₂ molecule fixed. The cyclic pathway tops up the extra ATP.
It also runs when NADP⁺ is in short supply because most of it is already loaded as NADPH. The energised electrons then still have somewhere to go.
notes.tip: The classic mistake is saying the cyclic pathway makes NADPH or oxygen. It makes ATP only, because water is never split.

notes.h: Comparing the two pathways (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Exams ask you to tell the two pathways apart. The differences all come back to one thing: where the electrons end up.
points: Route of the electrons: non-cyclic goes one way, from water to NADP⁺; cyclic goes from the chlorophyll round the carriers and back to the same chlorophyll.
Final electron acceptor: NADP⁺ in the non-cyclic pathway; the chlorophyll molecule itself in the cyclic pathway.
Water: split by photolysis in the non-cyclic pathway, to replace the lost electrons; not needed in the cyclic pathway, because the electrons come back.
Products: non-cyclic makes ATP, NADPH and oxygen; cyclic makes ATP only.

What they share: both start with light energy reaching the reaction centre and an energised electron leaving the chlorophyll, both pass electrons along carriers to make ATP, and both happen on the thylakoid membranes.

Older Irish textbooks and past papers call the cyclic pathway pathway 1 and the non-cyclic pathway pathway 2, and describe NADP⁺ becoming NADP⁻ before it picks up a proton. Recognise these names, but learn the single step to NADPH given above.

Diagram: one energy diagram with chlorophyll at the bottom receiving light from pigment molecules; the electron rising to an acceptor; a downhill chain (ATP made) ending at NADP⁺ → NADPH; water entering below the chlorophyll; a loop back to the chlorophyll for the cyclic pathway (ATP made).
notes.tip: When asked to distinguish, give paired points, one for each pathway, covering electron route, products and whether water is split.

notes.h: Summary of the light-dependent reactions (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Put together, the light-dependent reactions turn light into a form of energy the rest of the chloroplast can use, and hand it on to the second stage.
points: Location: the thylakoid membranes (grana) of the chloroplast, because that is where the pigments and electron carriers are held.
Inputs: light energy, water, ADP + Pi and NADP⁺.
Outputs: ATP and NADPH, which pass into the stroma for the light-independent reactions, and oxygen, released as a by-product.
Energy conversion: light energy becomes chemical energy, stored in ATP and in the high-energy electrons carried by NADPH.

The two products have different jobs: ATP carries energy, and NADPH carries electrons and hydrogen to reduce carbon dioxide to glucose. After use, they return as ADP + Pi and NADP⁺ to be reloaded. There is more on this in The light-independent reactions.
notes.tip: If asked what passes from the light stage to the light-independent stage, name both and give each one's role: ATP supplies energy, NADPH supplies electrons and hydrogen.

keyTerms.definition: A tiny packet of light energy, absorbed by pigment molecules in the light-dependent reactions.
The special chlorophyll a molecule, surrounded by pigment clusters, where light energy excites an electron that leaves the chlorophyll.
The splitting of water molecules, driven by the positively charged chlorophyll, into protons, electrons and oxygen.
The route in which electrons pass from water through the chlorophyll and the electron transport chain to NADP⁺, producing ATP, NADPH and oxygen.
The route in which energised electrons return to the same chlorophyll after passing along the carriers, producing ATP only.
A series of electron carriers that pass electrons from one to the next, releasing energy in small steps that is used to make ATP.
The electron and hydrogen carrier formed when NADP⁺ takes two electrons and one proton; it carries these to the light-independent reactions.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the cyclic and non-cyclic pathways of the light-dependent reactions.
questions.model: In the cyclic pathway, energised electrons leave the reaction-centre chlorophyll, pass along the carriers of the electron transport chain and return to the same chlorophyll, instead of going to NADP⁺. Surplus energy from them is used to make ATP, and ATP is the only product. In the non-cyclic pathway, electrons travel one way, from water through the chlorophyll and the chain to NADP⁺, so this pathway makes ATP, NADPH and oxygen. Water is split by photolysis only in the non-cyclic pathway; in the cyclic pathway water is not split, so no oxygen is released and no NADPH is made.

questions.prompt: Describe the events of the non-cyclic pathway, from the absorption of a photon to the production of NADPH and oxygen.
questions.model: A photon of light is absorbed by a pigment molecule in a light-harvesting cluster of pigments such as chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b and carotenoids. The energy is passed from one pigment molecule to the next until it reaches the reaction centre, a special chlorophyll a molecule. There it excites an electron to a high energy level, and the energised electron leaves the chlorophyll and is taken up by the first electron acceptor of an electron transport chain. The chlorophyll, having lost an electron, is left positively charged. The electrons pass along the chain of carriers in the thylakoid membrane, losing some energy at each transfer, and this energy is used to make ATP from ADP and Pi. At the end of the chain the electrons are passed to NADP⁺, which takes two electrons and one proton (H⁺) to form NADPH. Meanwhile the positively charged chlorophyll attracts electrons strongly and pulls them from water molecules, splitting the water by photolysis: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂. The electrons from water replace those lost by the chlorophyll, which becomes neutral again and can absorb more energy. The oxygen is released as a by-product.

questions.prompt: Explain why a chloroplast needs the cyclic pathway as well as the non-cyclic pathway.
questions.model: The non-cyclic pathway produces ATP, NADPH and oxygen, but the light-independent reactions use more ATP than NADPH, in a ratio of 3 ATP to 2 NADPH for each CO₂ molecule fixed. The cyclic pathway makes extra ATP from the surplus energy of electrons that return to the chlorophyll, which tops up the supply of ATP for the light-independent reactions. The cyclic pathway is also needed when NADP⁺ is in short supply, because most of it is already loaded as NADPH; the energised electrons then still have an acceptor, the chlorophyll itself, so they are not lost. The cyclic pathway produces ATP only, so it supplements the non-cyclic supply rather than replacing it.
